params.text:
Confidentiality and the Caldicott principles

Confidentiality means keeping personal information private and only using or sharing it appropriately. In health and social care, the Caldicott principles guide how confidential information is handled. In practice they ask you to:

  • Justify the purpose — be clear why you need the information for every use.
  • Use it only when necessary — do not use confidential information unless it is genuinely required.
  • Use the minimum necessary — share no more than is needed, never gathering information ‘just in case’.
  • Access on a need-to-know basis — people should see only the information their role requires.
  • Understand your responsibilities — everyone handling confidential information must know their duties and comply with the law.
  • Be open — organisations should be transparent with people about how their information is used, so there are no surprises.
  • Share when it is right to — the duty to share information can be as important as the duty to protect it.

A Caldicott Guardian is a senior person in many services who champions the confidential and appropriate use of people’s information.

Need to know and the duty to share

‘Need to know’ is a practical test: before you look at, discuss or pass on information, ask whether you actually need it to do your job or keep someone safe. Curiosity is never a good enough reason.

At the same time, protecting information is not the same as hoarding it. One Caldicott principle makes clear that the duty to share can be as important as the duty to protect. If a person could be harmed because professionals held back information that should have been shared, that failure is just as serious as an inappropriate disclosure. Safe, joined-up care depends on getting this balance right — and on recording your reasons.

params.textField: You should use the *minimum* amount of confidential information needed, and only access records on a strict need-to-*know* basis. Every use of that information must have a justified *purpose*. One principle reminds us that the duty to *share* can be as important as the duty to protect, so that people receive safe, joined-up *care*.
